card.hook: Here's a fun one: Dejima was an island, and now it isn't. It's a tiny patch of old Nagasaki, about 120 m by 75 m, tucked into the modern city.
card.stand_here: Stand near 出嶋橋, at the phone icon on the map, about 20 m east of the subject, and face west. Take a wide first look at the whole site before you walk in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big scene. If you move closer and things don't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for roof edges, doorways and signs.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the building you want so the pale walls don't get lost against the sky.
card.best_time: Go in the morning. The sun is in the east behind you when you face west, so the front of the site is nicely lit. Cloudy days work too, because the light is soft and the walls don't get harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Head to the restored Omotemon Bridge, the entrance bridge to Dejima. It's a popular photo backdrop with the Nagasaki skyline behind it. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and turn so the scenery sits over your shoulder. For something different, pose in front of the sky-blue former Dejima Seminary, which is part of the Dejima Museum.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the near end of Omotemon Bridge, where visitors enter, while you stand on the bridge for the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the site may be ticketed or have set visiting times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots: the whole site, one with a doorway or wall framing the edge, then one tiny detail. Which one would you put on the fridge?
card.good_to_know: Dejima was built in 1636 to hold foreign traders. For 220 years it was Japan's main link with the West, and the Dutch were based here from 1641 until 1858. It became a national historic site in 1922, and work continues to bring back its island setting.

card.hook: This isn't a spot for a showy photo, and that's fine. Step back into the park and the museum's calm, orderly walls settle into the frame all by themselves.
card.stand_here: The phone icon is right at the museum, so walk out into Nagasaki Peace Park, then turn around and face the building. You'll have plenty of room to fit the walls in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the building as you see it. If you're close and can't fit the whole front in, tap 0.5x. Zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) is good for details like the entrance or the lines of the walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building's edges up with them so the walls look straight, then tap the building and slide a touch darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Soft or evenly overcast daylight gives the cleanest, least glaring pictures. Earlier or quieter parts of the day usually mean fewer people in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Try the wide stairs climbing from Hypocenter Park up to the museum. Stand on the steps facing back down toward the park, so the museum should be behind you, and use the front camera. Keep it simple and unposed, since this is a place of mourning for many visitors. Check the building behind you before you shoot, because a large red-brick building nearby is a different institution.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the foot of the stairs in Hypocenter Park while you stand on the steps, so the museum building rises above you.
card.rules_and_safety: Outdoor photography in Peace Park and Hypocenter Park is unrestricted, but photography is banned in the Remembrance Hall. Inside the museum, photos are allowed without flash or selfie sticks, and two specific works can't be photographed (the painting at the B2 ticket machines and the 'Boy Standing by the Crematory' photo at the B1 exit). Check the official site before you go and follow any signs in the galleries.
card.challenge: Get the walls dead straight on your gridlines with a little open sky above, and no strangers' faces in the shot.
card.good_to_know: The museum remembers the atomic bombing of Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, at 11:02 in the morning. It was completed in April 1996 and replaced the older International Culture Hall, where relics were first shown. Next door is the Nagasaki National Peace Memorial Hall for the Atomic Bomb Victims, built in 2003. One object inside is a clock stopped at 11:02.

card.hook: Everything in this park sits on one long, calm line: a fountain at one end, a huge statue at the other, and sculptures in between. That makes it an easy place to take a photo that feels quiet and uncluttered.
card.stand_here: Stand near 国道206号, about 55 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The path stretches out ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the long view up the park. Try 0.5x if you want more sky and sculpture in the shot. Use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for faces, plaques and the Peace Statue from a distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the main path on one of the lines so it leads the eye into the park.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. Around 9 August, the day of the annual ceremony, it's much busier and more formal.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x so you and the scene behind you both fit. Hold the phone a little higher, keep the pose calm and simple, and let the park sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a place of remembrance, so keep your phone use quiet and unhurried and avoid posing in a way that would feel out of place. There may be restrictions around events and ceremonies, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and take one shot with the path leading to a statue, then one close-up of a detail like the fountain plaque.
card.good_to_know: The park opened in 1955 to remember the atomic bombing of 9 August 1945. The bomb exploded 500 metres up at 11:02 that morning, and a black stone monolith marks the spot beneath it. The 10-metre Peace Statue is by Nagasaki sculptor Seibo Kitamura, and the Fountain of Peace was built in 1969.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near 国道206号, about 55 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The path stretches out ahead of you.

card.hook: Imagine building your house on a hill so the whole of Nagasaki harbour is your front yard. That's Glover Garden, and the old Western-style houses here make the view even better.
card.stand_here: Stand near グラバー通り, at the phone icon on the map, about 80 m north of the subject, and face south. If other visitors are in the way, walk a few steps along the path for a cleaner angle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole garden and the harbour beyond. Switch to 1x for the houses and paths, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the demon-headed roof tiles, chimneys and statues.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the house, then slide the brightness down a little if the sky is bright, so the white walls and roof tiles keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day usually means softer light and fewer people. Check the official site for opening times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the highest point of the garden and stand in front of the second floor of the Former Mitsubishi No. 2 Dock House, which guides recommend for commemorative photos and call the widest panorama in the garden. Or step onto the Former Glover House veranda with the harbour behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it to squeeze in more of the view over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lawn or path in front of the former Glover House so the whole house fills the frame, with you posing in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask staff before taking photos inside the old houses, and check the official site for entry arrangements before you go.
card.challenge: Play roof detective: find the demon-headed tiles, then get one close-up shot where the demons are the stars and not you.
card.good_to_know: The Glover Residence was completed in 1863 and is the oldest surviving Western-style house in Japan. It was built by a Japanese carpenter, Hidenoshin Koyama, so the frame is Japanese while the stone-floored verandas and French windows are foreign touches. It's nicknamed the "Madame Butterfly House", and statues of Puccini and the singer Miura Tamaki stand nearby.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near グラバー通り, at the phone icon on the map, about 80 m north of the subject, and face south. If other visitors are in the way, walk a few steps along the path for a cleaner angle.

card.hook: Picture two brick-coloured towers sitting calmly on a hill above the neighbourhood, looking far too peaceful for what they've been through. That's Urakami Cathedral, and it's one of those photos that means more once you know the story.
card.stand_here: Head to Nagasaki Peace Park (平和公園) and stand beyond the Peace Statue, on the far side of the park. Face the cathedral on its hill, with the neighbourhood spread out below it.
card.zoom: From the park the cathedral looks small at 1x, so try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring it closer. Walk up to the grounds and drop back to 1x. Use 0.5x only if you're right in front and want both towers and the entrance in one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and hold your phone level so the towers stand straight, and if the sky is bright and the brickwork looks dark, tap the cathedral front and drag the slider to make it a bit brighter.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the brick-coloured walls and skips harsh midday shadows. Early in the day you'll probably have fewer people in your frame too.
card.selfie_here: Once you're in the grounds, try the front entrance beside the statues of the Grieving Virgin and St. John, with the façade behind you. Or go to the blasted bell tower ruins by the stream on the left side of the cathedral. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Peace Park platform that looks over the cathedral to take your photo, so you stand with the cathedral view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Visitor pages say photography isn't allowed inside the cathedral. Ask before photographing anyone, skip photos during worship, and during Mass wait outside or come back later. The walk up is steep, which can be tough if you have mobility issues.
card.challenge: Get both towers dead straight against the gridlines, then take a second shot of the bell or the Atom-bombed Mary to tell the whole story.
card.good_to_know: Local Christians, whose faith had been banned and who were sent into exile between 1869 and 1873, began building the first cathedral in 1895. When it was finished in 1925 it was the largest Christian building in the Asia-Pacific region. The atomic bomb of 9 August 1945 destroyed it. The congregation rebuilt on the same site, finishing in October 1959, and in 1980 the walls were re-faced with brick tiles to look more like the original.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Nagasaki Peace Park (平和公園) and stand beyond the Peace Statue, on the far side of the park. Face the cathedral on its hill, with the neighbourhood spread out below it.

card.hook: You huff your way up a long stone staircase (often given as 277 steps, though counts vary), and then you turn around and the whole city is sitting there inside a red frame. That's your reward.
card.stand_here: Stand on the gate (大門), right where the phone icon is on the map, and face out over the city. The vermilion approach runs in front of you and the rooftops spread out below.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate and the view through it. Go to 0.5x to squeeze the approach and the city into one frame, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out rooftops below.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky or city, then slide it a touch darker so the lit scene doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Evening or after dusk is lovely, when the stone steps are lit and the city lights come on. Check opening arrangements first, as the long torii walkway may close after normal visiting hours.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the right of the entrance and climb a few more steps to the small torii garden. A reviewer found it quiet, so use the front camera and put the torii behind you. If it's busy, go around the side and back of the main temple, where more torii stand, and try 0.5x to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone near the main entrance by the bottom torii gate, at the foot of the steps, to take your photo with the torii behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine outdoors, but check for signs inside buildings, and skip photos during ceremonies or of people praying. It's a working place of worship, so keep your voice down and don't block the path. The steps can be a bit rocky, so watch your feet.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and line the red gate edges up straight, then see if you can get the city sitting neatly in the frame without a wonky tilt.
card.good_to_know: Suwa Shrine is the main Shinto shrine of Nagasaki. Its official founding date is 1614, and the main building was completed in 1626. It was still standing after the atomic bombing of 9 August 1945, and every year on 7 to 9 October it hosts the Nagasaki Kunchi, one of Japan's major festivals.

card.hook: Walk up to Sōfuku-ji and you'll wonder if you took a wrong turn into China. The bright red Ryugamon, the 'Gate of the Dragon Palace', looks nothing like most Japanese temple gates.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 20 m north of the subject, and face south toward the red gate. Take your first wide shot from here, then move in closer.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate and main buildings as you see them. If the courtyard is too tight to fit a whole building in, tap 0.5x. For roof ends, carvings and lanterns, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red paintwork, then slide the brightness down a touch so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the red paint and carved timber. The temple is listed as open daily 8am to 5pm, but check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Climb the roughly 50 steps from the two-story tower gate up to the Daiippōmon inner gate, then turn back toward the first gate below. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the gate over your shoulder. It's the closest documented photo spot here, so have a play with the angle.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine in the grounds, but check for signs inside buildings, as some areas or objects may be off limits. It's an active temple, so be considerate of people praying and keep out of doorways and paths.
card.challenge: Find the big cauldron Qianhai made for the 1681 famine and get a shot that makes it look as huge as it is.
card.good_to_know: Chinese monk Chaoran founded Sōfuku-ji in 1629 as the family temple for people from Fuzhou living in Nagasaki. The Daiyū Hōden Buddha Hall is one of the city's oldest buildings: its sections were cut in China, shipped over and assembled here in 1646. The current red gate dates from 1849, and two of the temple's buildings are national treasures.

card.hook: Oura Church is a gift for phone photos: pale walls, a steep roofline and one octagonal tower that stands out like it knows you're coming.
card.stand_here: Stand about 45 m north-east of the church, at the phone icon on the map near グラバーヒル, and face south-west. From here the whole building fits in the frame, with a bit of its surroundings.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole church in. Try 2x to pick out the tower and façade from this distance. Save 0.5x for when you walk closer, because it makes the building look narrow at the top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the church wall, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white walls keep their detail instead of going pale.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer on the white walls and the courtyard is usually quieter. Check the church's opening times before you plan your visit.
card.selfie_here: Climb the church steps and turn to face back down toward the harbour and the old streets, so the church is behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little high, then try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the church over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sloping path called kinen-zaka ('prayer's slope') that curves around the side of the church, since it gives a classic white façade shot, best in morning light.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear sturdy shoes, as the approach has slopes. This is a working Catholic church and heritage site that may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Line the tower up on a gridline so it stands perfectly straight, then walk closer and catch one small detail, like a window or the bronze relief in the courtyard.
card.good_to_know: A small wooden church was finished here in 1864 for the French community. The larger church you see now dates from around 1878, with stained glass brought from France. In March 1865, villagers from nearby Urakami came to the doors and quietly told the priest they shared his faith, and a bronze relief in the courtyard shows the scene.

card.hook: Imagine turning in a slow circle and seeing a whole city, its harbour and the mountains behind it, without moving your feet. That's the rooftop on Mount Inasa, the classic place to look back over Nagasaki.
card.stand_here: Head for the observation deck near the summit of Mount Inasa. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, a short walk from the top stations of the ropeway and the slope car. Face the city, then turn around on the deck to pick your view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the main city view, then try 0.5x on the rooftop to squeeze more of the 360-degree scene in. Use 2x or 5x to pick out details like the harbour or a single hillside.
card.make_it_pop: After dark, turn on night mode, rest your elbows on the rail, tap a bright patch of city, then slide it a little darker so the lights don't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into evening is perfect. Shoot the daytime view first, then stay on while the city lights come on, because the whole scene changes.
card.selfie_here: Use the open-air rooftop terrace of the Mount Inasa Observatory, not the indoor glass level, since the open roof avoids glass reflections. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the city lights over your shoulder. The deck wraps right around the building, so if one side is busy, walk round to a quieter section.
card.rules_and_safety: The observation deck may have its own entry arrangements, so check the official site before you go. Shoot over the rail only where that's allowed.
card.challenge: Take the same view twice, once in daylight and once after dark, and see which one wins.
card.good_to_know: Mount Inasa rises to 333 metres on the west side of Nagasaki. Its outlook is called the "10 Million Dollar Night View", and Nagasaki's night view was named one of the "World's New Three Great Night Views" in 2021. Inasayama Park, with a playground, outdoor stage and lawn seating, is on the mountain too.

card.hook: Picture a bridge wearing glasses: two stone arches, and when the water's calm, two mirror-image circles underneath. That's Megane Bridge, and the reflection is the whole point.
card.stand_here: Start near 袋橋, about 70 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You'll see the whole bridge and its reflection in one frame, then you can stroll closer.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit both arches and their reflection. Use 0.5x only if you have to stand very close, and keep the bridge away from the edges of the screen so it doesn't stretch. For the heart-shaped stones, try 2x or higher (depends on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the water's surface up with a horizontal line so the arches and reflection sit level, and leave a little water in the foreground so the reflected circles stay complete.
card.best_time: Pick a moment when the water is calm, because that's when the reflection is clearest. Early morning or late afternoon is often gentler on stone and water than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head down the stone steps to the water's edge beside Fukurobashi, just downstream of the bridge, and get low with the arches behind you. Use the front camera, or switch to 0.5x to squeeze in more bridge over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on Fukurobashi and ask a passer-by to shoot upstream, so the whole of Megane Bridge and its reflection fit in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is pedestrians only, but check the official site before you go in case of works or flood closures.
card.challenge: Find the small heart-shaped stones in the embankment (there are around twenty) and see how many you can spot in one close-up.
card.good_to_know: Megane Bridge was built in 1634 by Mokusu Nyojo, a Chinese monk who lived at Kofukuji Temple. It's said to be one of the oldest stone arch bridges in Japan and is an Important Cultural Property. A flood destroyed it in 1647 and it was rebuilt the next year, and after a severe flood in July 1982 nearly all the original stones were recovered and put back.

card.hook: Picture a street so packed with red, gold and food stalls that you can go from a wide street scene to a close-up of a sign in about a minute. That's Nagasaki Shinchi Chinatown, and the whole area is only about 253 m across.
card.stand_here: Stand near 福建通り, about 75 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. The street will lead your eye straight down the shopfronts.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the street view. Switch to zoom 0.5x for a gate or a whole row of shopfronts, and keep the phone level so the edges don't stretch. Try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for lanterns, signs and food, so you don't have to step into the stalls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the buildings and posts so the street looks straight, with shopfronts on both sides.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening is lovely, because shop lighting and lanterns glow as the daylight fades. Mornings are likely to be quieter if you want clearer street views.

card.rules_and_safety: It can get busy, so keep an eye on the crowds and keep a little space around shopfronts and stalls. Ask before you photograph people at close range.
card.challenge: Find three different bits of red in the street, take one close-up of each, then see which one wins.
card.good_to_know: The land here was once used for the warehouses of Chinese merchants, who traded goods to Japan between the 15th and 19th centuries. Nagasaki was the only port the Tokugawa government left open to Chinese and Dutch traders. Most of today's Chinese community here is of Fuzhounese descent, and Nagasaki became a sister city of Fuzhou in 1980.

card.hook: The Peace Statue is a simple shape against a big sky, and that's what makes it so easy to photograph. You don't need fancy settings, just a little patience and a calm moment.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 25 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. That's far enough back to fit the whole figure in with some space around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a clean, natural view of the statue. Try 0.5x only if you want the statue and its surroundings together, and keep the statue away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. For a closer shot of the figure, use 2x or 5x if your phone has them.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the statue's base on a lower line so the figure rises into the sky, and hold your phone level so it doesn't seem to lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can be harsh and cast hard shadows on the statue.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, hold your arm out a little low, and let the statue rise over your shoulder. If your front camera has 0.5x, it helps fit more in. Keep your pose calm, because this is a place of remembrance.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the plaza at the north end of Peace Park, facing the statue, because standing straight in front gives the most complete view of the full figure.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed in most outdoor areas of Peace Park, but please stay respectful and keep your voice down. Don't climb on the sculptures or monuments, and note that photos are strictly prohibited in the Memorial Hall inside the Atomic Bomb Museum. Check the official site before you go for any access rules or closures.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the statue small in the sky, then one close shot of just the figure, and see which one feels calmer.
card.good_to_know: The Peace Statue is a memorial figure in Nagasaki. People come to photograph it as a reminder of the city's history. It's a large, simple subject that stands out cleanly against the sky, so it works well on a phone.

card.hook: Half a gate shouldn't be this powerful, but one pillar and a beam floating above it against the sky stops people mid-step. Come quietly and give it a moment.
card.stand_here: Head to Sannō Shrine, about 800 metres south-east of the atomic bomb hypocentre, and stand at the phone icon at the top of the stone steps. Face the one-legged torii so the pillar and beam fill your view against the sky.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the gate looks natural, and keep your phone upright so the pillar looks tall. If you can't step back far enough to fit the whole gate, try zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x for a closer shot of the beam and pillar.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the torii, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the gate turns into a clean silhouette.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest, because the clear sky behind the torii makes the shape stand out. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer visitors.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the stone staircase below the one-legged torii, with the gate behind you as you face down the slope. Use the front camera and hold it low, since low angles make the gate look more imposing. Try zoom 0.5x if you can't fit the whole gate over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street at the bottom of the stone steps, far enough back to fit the whole torii above you, while you stand on the steps below the gate.
card.rules_and_safety: The torii is fenced off and you can't walk through it, so photograph it from outside the fence. This is a place of remembrance, so keep it calm and quiet, and don't block the steps or path. Go in daylight, as there's uphill walking and stairs.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the whole gate in the frame so the missing half is clear. Then walk over to the camphor trees and fill the frame with the healed, layered bark.
card.good_to_know: The torii was damaged by the atomic bomb blast on 9 August 1945. One pillar was knocked down, but the other stayed upright with its upper beam still on top. The shockwave also turned the gate about 30 degrees on its base. The shrine's two big camphor trees were scorched and lost their leaves, yet they survived, and new growth now covers the dead wood.

card.hook: The last stretch up Nishizaka Hill is steep, and then the climb pays off: a wide bronze wall of figures, with Nagasaki's rooftops spread out beside it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the open square in front of the monument, at the top of the hill, and face the bronze so the rooftops sit behind or beside it. Turn around later for the city view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole bronze and the rooftops, then switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for faces and hands.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the monument on one third of the frame, then tap the bronze and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, so both the bronze and the town show up well.
card.selfie_here: Use the open square in front of the monument. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the bronze over your shoulder. Keep it quick and quiet, because this is a memorial.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the square along the straight red line running out from the monument and shoot back toward it, while you stand in front of the bronze so it fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine in the outdoor park for personal use, but the museum may have its own rules, and flash is often banned there. Keep voices low and don't block people who've come to pay their respects. The hill is steep, so take the climb slowly.
card.challenge: Find one small detail in the bronze, like a hand or a face, and fill your whole screen with it.
card.good_to_know: This memorial honours 26 Christians put to death here on 5 February 1597: twenty Japanese and six foreign priests, who had walked to Nagasaki after being arrested in Kyoto and Osaka. The monument and museum opened in June 1962, and sculptor Yasutake Funakoshi spent four years on the bronze. Next door, St Philip's Church is built in the style of Gaudí, so its shapes make a good second subject.

card.hook: Picture a yellow-tiled gate with dragons on the roof and 72 stone statues lined up like they're waiting for the doors to open. It's a very different Nagasaki from the rest of your camera roll.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in front of the Gimon gate (the yellow-tiled front gate), and face the gate with its dragon roof ornaments. Walk closer when you want the statue shots.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the main building. Switch to 0.5x if you're close and want the whole frontage and the row of statues in one shot. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for roof and doorway details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the roofline level, then tap the brightest coloured wall and slide it a touch darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the frame. Check opening times on the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Climb the steep stone bridge over the small pond in front of the Gimon gate, use the front camera, and keep the yellow-roofed gate with its dragons behind you. For a second option, stand among the 72 statues in the courtyard in front of the main hall (Taiseiden) and let the hall sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the garden path at the near side of the pond and shoot toward the bridge while you stand on the bridge, so you and the gate both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the statues and the grounds are generally fine, but photography inside the museum isn't permitted. Check the signs when you arrive, as the rules can vary.
card.challenge: Crouch down, line up a few statues in a row, and make them lead your eye straight to the shrine.
card.good_to_know: Chinese residents of Nagasaki built the shrine in 1893, with support from the Qing dynasty government, as a place of worship and learning. The atomic bomb badly damaged it on 9 August 1945, and it reopened in September 1967 before a big renovation in 1982. The land is now owned by the Chinese Embassy in Tokyo, and a museum of Chinese history sits in the building at the rear.

card.hook: At 320 m away, Megami Bridge isn't about one clever detail. It's the whole scene, and that makes it perfect for a wide photo to drop into your album or send home.
card.stand_here: Stand about 320 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. The bridge will be right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full view. If the bridge looks small, try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot. Only use 0.5x if you walk closer and want the whole length of the bridge in one picture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the bridge up along one of the horizontal lines so it sits level, with a little sky or water around it.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day with the sun behind you or off to one side, so the bridge is lit rather than dark. Early morning or later in the day often gives softer light.
card.selfie_here: Head to the waterfront promenade in Nagasaki Seaside Park, where the bridge is in the distance across the bay. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone so the bridge is over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Up at the Mt. Nabekanmuri Park Observatory (the mountain behind Glover Garden), ask a passer-by to take your photo with Nagasaki Port and Mt. Inasa behind you, where the bridge is seen up close.
card.rules_and_safety: On the bridge's footpath the wind can be quite strong, so dress warmly in winter. Take care near any road or path, and keep clear of traffic while you frame your shot.
card.challenge: Take three frames and see if you can get the bridge perfectly level on the gridline in at least one of them.
card.good_to_know: Megami Bridge is number 19 on the Nagasaki map. We don't have history, size or opening dates for it, so we're sticking to photo advice. If you want to get closer, the bridge is south-west of the phone icon, about 318 m in a straight line.
